questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with numbness and tingling along the lateral aspect of his forearm and thumb following a fall on his outstretched arm. Which dermatome is most likely involved?

explanation.text: The C6 dermatome covers the lateral aspect of the forearm, the thumb, and part of the index finger. Numbness or tingling in this area, suggests involvement of the C6 dermatome.

Dermatomes of the Upper Limb: Spinal Nerve Root Dermatome (Sensory Area) C5 (Option A ruled out) Lateral upper arm, over the deltoid C6 (Option B) Lateral forearm and thumb(1st digit) C7 (Option C ruled out) Index finger (2nd digit) to Ring finger (4th digit) C8 (Option D ruled out) Medial forearm, little finger (5th digit) T1 Medial arm and elbow

questions.question: A 40-year-old male presents with difficulty extending his elbow after a recent injury. On examination, you notice weakness in elbow extension and diminished triceps reflex. Sensory examination is normal. Which myotome is most likely affected?

explanation.text: The C7 myotome innervates the triceps muscle, which is responsible for elbow extension.

Myotomes of the Upper Limb: Spinal Nerve Root Myotome (Motor Function) C5 (Option A ruled out) Shoulder abduction (deltoid), elbow flexion (biceps) C6 (Option B ruled out) Elbow flexion, wrist extension (biceps, wrist extensors) C7 (Option C) Elbow extension (triceps), wrist flexion (wrist flexors) C8 (Option D ruled out) Finger flexion, thumb extension (finger flexors, intrinsic hand muscles) T1 Finger abduction and adduction (intrinsic hand muscles, interossei)

questions.question: A 25-year-old male presents with weakness in the upper limb following a fall on his shoulder. Physical examination reveals impaired movement in the extensor muscles of the arm. Injury to which part of the brachial plexus is most likely responsible for this patient's symptoms?

explanation.text: The posterior divisions of the brachial plexus innervate the extensor muscles of the upper limb. The middle trunk is a direct continuation of the C7 ventral ramus and its posterior division supplies the extensor muscles. Brachial Plexus Trunks: Formation: Five ventral rami (C5–T1) form three trunks. Upper Trunk: Formed by C5 and C6. Middle Trunk: Continuation of C7. Lower Trunk: Formed by C8 and T1, crossing over the first rib.

Location: Trunks emerge between anterior and middle scalene muscles. Positioned anteriorly to each other, with the subclavian artery running anteromedially. Divisions: Each trunk divides into: Posterior Divisions: Innervate extensor muscles. Anterior Divisions: Innervate flexor muscles. Clinical Relevance: Trunks, especially the upper trunk, can be palpated in the supraclavicular fossa. Important for procedures like nerve blocks.

Brachial Plexus Trunk Formation and Divisions: Trunk Formation Divisions Upper Trunk Union of C5 and C6 rami Anterior: Flexor muscles (Option A ruled out) Posterior: Extensor muscles Middle Trunk Continuation of C7 Anterior: Flexor muscles (Option B ruled out) Posterior: Extensor muscles (Option C) Lower Trunk Union of C8 and T1 rami Anterior: Flexor muscles (Option A ruled out) Passing over first rib Posterior: Extensor muscles

questions.question: A 25-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motorcycle accident. He complains of severe pain and weakness in his right arm. On examination, there is loss of sensation in the right shoulder and upper arm with weakness in shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. Which of the following is the most likely type of brachial plexus lesion in this patient?

explanation.text: Closed traction injury commonly occurs due to violent forces, such as those experienced in high-speed accidents, which stretch or tear the nerves of the brachial plexus. The symptoms of pain, weakness, and sensory loss in this patient are consistent with this type of lesion. Brachial Plexus Lesions: Damage or dysfunction in the brachial plexus, a nerve network from the spinal cord controlling shoulder, arm, and hand functions.

Causes of Brachial Plexus Lesions include: Trauma, birth trauma, tumors, radiation therapy Types of Lesions: Type Description Closed Traction Lesions (Option C) Result from forces that stretch or tear nerves, often in high-impact incidents like accidents.
**Intradural Ruptures/Avulsions (Option A ruled out):** Nerve roots torn from the spinal cord; harder to treat than other injuries.

**Compression Injuries (Option B ruled out):** Caused by pressure on the brachial plexus, including: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome (TOS): Compression between the clavicle and first rib. Hematoma: Internal bleeding compressing the plexus. Anomalous Muscles/Structures: Extra anatomical features causing compression. Iatrogenic Injury: Damage during medical procedures. (Option D ruled out) Symptoms: Symptom Description Sensory Changes Numbness, tingling, pain, or burning in the shoulder, arm, or hand. Motor Weakness Difficulty moving the shoulder, arm, or hand, with specific weakness patterns aiding localization. Autonomic Dysfunction Changes in sweating, skin temperature, or blood flow in the affected limb. Diagnosis: Physical Exam: Assessing sensation, muscle strength, and reflexes. Imaging Studies: X-rays, CT scans, or MRI to identify fractures, dislocations, or tumors. Electrodiagnostic Tests: Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) to assess nerve function and damage extent.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male presents with weakness in elbow flexion and loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of his forearm. Which of the following nerves is most likely involved in this patient’s condition?

explanation.text: The musculocutaneous nerve innervates the biceps brachii and brachialis muscles, responsible for elbow flexion. It also provides sensory innervation to the lateral aspect of the forearm. Brachial Plexus: Brachial plexus: Nerve network for upper limb motor and sensory function. Origins: From ventral rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1 spinal nerves. Structure: Roots → trunks → divisions → cords.
Function: Specific nerves innervate muscles and skin in the arm and hand.

Brachial Plexus Cords: Cord Formation Lateral Cord Anterior divisions of upper and middle trunks Posterior Cord All three posterior divisions Medial Cord Anterior division of lower trunk (sometimes middle trunk) Innervations by Cord: Cord Nerve Motor Innervation Sensory Innervation Lateral Cord Musculocutaneous (C5, C6, C7) (Option B) Biceps brachii, brachialis, coracobrachialis Lateral forearm Lateral Root of Median (C5, C6, C7) Contributes to median nerve (primarily hand muscles) Contributes to sensory innervation of the hand Posterior Cord Axillary (C5, C6) (Option A ruled out) Deltoid, teres minor Lateral shoulder Radial (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1) (Option C ruled out) Triceps, brachioradialis, wrist and finger extensors, supinator Posterior arm, forearm, dorsolateral hand Upper Subscapular (C5, C6) Subscapularis None Thoracodorsal (C6, C7, C8) Latissimus dorsi None Lower Subscapular (C5, C6) Subscapularis, teres major None Medial Cord Ulnar (C8, T1) (Option D ruled out) Flexor carpi ulnaris, flexor digitorum profundus (medial half), most intrinsic hand muscles Medial hand, little finger, medial half of ring finger Median (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1) Pronators, wrist/finger flexors (except those supplied by ulnar), thenar muscles Palmar hand (thumb, index, middle, lateral half of ring finger) Medial Pectoral (C8, T1) Pectoralis major, pectoralis minor None Medial Cutaneous Nerve of Arm (C8, T1) None Medial arm Medial Cutaneous Nerve of Forearm (C8, T1) None Medial forearm

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the variations in the prefixed and postfixed brachial plexus?

options.A: Prefixed brachial plexus is characterized by contributions from C5 to T2.
options.B: T2 spinal nerve replaces the usual T1 contribution in postfixed brachial plexus.
options.C: Prefixed brachial plexus has an increased contribution from C4 and decreased from T1.
options.D: Postfixed brachial plexus is associated with an increased contribution from C3 and C4.

explanation.text: A prefixed brachial plexus has an increased contribution from C4 and decreased from T1 while a postfixed brachial plexus involves contributions from C6-T2, with diminished input from C5 and increased input from T2. The variations are significant in clinical practice as they can affect the innervation patterns of the upper limb and may impact nerve injury presentations.

Prefixed Postfixed Nerve root C4-C8 C6-T2 Shift Upward shift Downward shift C4 contribution Increased Nil or minimal C5 contribution Normal Reduced T1 contribution Reduced or nil Normal along with added T2 Risk No risk of compression High risk of compression (Thoracic outlet syndrome) Prefixed brachial plexus is characterized by contributions from C5 to T2 (Option A) is incorrect as in a prefixed brachial plexus, the contribution shifts upward, involving C4-C8, not C5 to T2.
There is minimal or no input from T1 in a prefixed plexus.

**T2 spinal nerve replaces the usual T1 contribution in postfixed brachial plexus (Option B):** is incorrect as in a postfixed brachial plexus, the contribution extends downward and typically includes C6-T2, but T2 does not replace T1. Instead, T1 remains part of the plexus, and T2 provides an additional contribution.

**Postfixed brachial plexus is associated with an increased contribution from C3 and C4 (Option D):** is incorrect as a postfixed brachial plexus involves a downward shift, resulting in contributions from C6-T2. There is no involvement of C3 and C4, which are part of the cervical plexus, not the brachial plexus.

questions.question: Which part of the brachial plexus does not give off any branches?

explanation.text: The divisions of the brachial plexus (anterior and posterior) act as a passage for nerve fibers to reorganize and form cords but they themselves do not give rise to any branches.

Part of brachial plexus Branches Roots Dorsal scapular nerve - C5 Long thoracic nerve - C5 to C7 Trunks Suprascapular nerve - C5, C6 Nerve to subclavius - C5, C6 Division None Cords Lateral pectoral nerve (Lateral cord: C5 - C7) Upper subscapular nerve (Posterior cord: C5, C6) Thoracodorsal nerve (Posterior cord: C6 - C8) Lower subscapular nerve (Posterior cord: C5, C6) Medial pectoral nerve (Medial cord: C8, T1) Medial cutaneous nerve of arm (Medial cord: C8, T1) Medial cutaneous nerve of forearm (Medial cord: C8, T1) Terminal branches Musculocutaneous nerve (Lateral cord, C5-C7) Axillary nerve (Posterior cord, C5, C6) Radial nerve (Posterior cord, C5-T1) Median nerve (Lateral and Medial cords, C5-T1) Ulnar nerve (Medial cord, C8, T1)

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the anterior and posterior axial lines is correct?

options.A: Axial lines form as a result of limb rotational and elongation processes during embryogenesis
options.B: Axial lines divide dermatomes that are adjacent in the spinal nerve sequence
options.C: Overlapping of nerve supply can overlap across axial lines
options.D: Overlapping of Ventral and dorsal axial lines can occur

explanation.text: Axial lines are the dividing lines between dermatomes that are not adjacent in the spinal nerve sequence which are formed as a result of limb rotational and elongation processes during embryogenesis. Axial lines Axial lines are the dividing lines between dermatomes that are not adjacent in the spinal nerve sequence. Types Ventral Axial Line (on the anterior surface of the limb). Dorsal Axial Line (on the posterior surface of the limb).

Formation During embryological development, the limbs undergo lateral rotation (upper limb) or medial rotation (lower limb). This rotation creates a spiral arrangement of dermatomes and shifts certain dermatomes distally. Axial lines form as a result of these rotational and elongation processes. Significance Axial lines are important for understanding nerve injuries and mapping sensory deficits.
Across these lines, there is no overlap between dermatomes, so sensory loss in these areas can help pinpoint the exact nerve or spinal segment involved.

**Axial lines divide dermatomes that are adjacent in the spinal nerve sequence (Option B):** This is incorrect as axial lines do not divide adjacent dermatomes. Instead, they divide dermatomes from non-adjacent spinal nerve roots. Adjacent dermatomes (e.g., C5 and C6) overlap significantly, and no axial line exists between them. For example, the ventral axial line separates C5, C6 from C8, T1, and T2, which are non-adjacent segments.

**Overlapping of nerve supply can overlap across axial lines (Option C):** This is incorrect as one of the defining features of axial lines is that there is no overlap of dermatomes across them. While overlapping of adjacent dermatomes is common elsewhere (e.g., C5 overlaps with C6), this does not happen across axial lines.

**Overlapping of ventral and dorsal axial lines can occur (Option D):** This is incorrect as the ventral and dorsal axial lines are distinct anatomical landmarks and do not overlap. They are located on opposite surfaces of the limb: The ventral axial line is on the anterior (palmar) surface of the limb. The dorsal axial line is on the posterior (dorsal) surface of the limb.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a content of the cubital fossa?

explanation.text: Cubital Fossa: Triangular space present in front of distal humerus and elbow joint. Boundaries: Medially Lateral border of pronator teres Laterally Medial border of brachioradialis Apex Point of convergence of medial and lateral boundaries Base Imaginary line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of humerus.

Roof Formed by deep fascia and reinforced by bicipital aponeurosis.The deep fascia is continuity of brachial and antebrachial fascia. Floor Lower portion of brachialis forms the floor of the upper part of the fossa; the supinator muscle forms the floor of the lower part of the fossa. Contents of cubital fossa: Median nerve: Lies medial to the brachial artery in the fossa and is anterior to brachioradialis and posterior to bicipital aponeurosis.

Radial nerve: Enters the cubital region by passing forwards in interval between the brachialis and brachioradialis and then divides into superficial branch and deep branch (posterior interosseous nerve). Brachial artery: Centrally placed in fossa and divides into radial and ulnar arteries with immediate anterior relation is bicipital aponeurosis.

Tendon of the biceps brachii and bicipital aponeurosis Contents of cubital fossa from medial to lateral: (Mnemonic: MBBS) Median nerve Brachial artery Biceps brachii tendon Superficial branch of radial nerve

questions.question: Which of the following is a unique feature of the clavicle compared to other bones in the body?

options.A: It ossifies from both membranous and cartilaginous origins.
options.B: It articulates directly with the scapula without an intervening joint cavity.
options.C: It is the only bone in the body that does not have a medullary cavity.
options.D: It is entirely covered by the periosteum, unlike other bones.

explanation.text: The clavicle is unique among bones in the human body due to its dual ossification process: Intramembranous Ossification: The medial and lateral parts of the clavicle develop through intramembranous ossification. This process is typical for flat bones like the skull. Endochondral Ossification: The sternal end of the clavicle ossifies through endochondral ossification, which involves a cartilage template being replaced by bone.

This process is more common for long bones like the femur and humerus. Features of the Clavicle: Horizontally placed long bone (unique among long bones). Two primary centers of ossification develop during intrauterine life to form the shaft (most long bones have only one primary center). One secondary ossification center Subcutaneous throughout and easily palpable. Lacks a medullary cavity, unlike most long bones.
Parts of the Clavicle: Medial 2/3: Anterior convexity. Lateral 1/3: Anterior concavity. Junction of these segments is prone to fractures. Muscle
Attachments: Medial 2/3 (Anterior): Origin of Pectoralis Major. Lateral 1/3 (Anterior): Origin of Deltoid. Lateral 1/3 (Posterior): Insertion of Trapezius.

The clavicle articulates with the scapula at the acromioclavicular joint, which does have a joint cavity. (Option B) While it is true that the clavicle lacks a medullary cavity, it is not the only bone with this feature (Flat bones like the sternum and skull bones). (Option C) All bones in the body are covered by periosteum except at articular surfaces. This characteristic is not unique to the clavicle. (Option D)

questions.question: After a fall from a height with undue arm abduction, the patient presented as shown. Mark the wrong statement about this condition.

options.B: Complete clawing of hand is seen
options.C: Associated horner syndrome can be seen
options.D: Due to injury to lower trunk of brachial plexus

explanation.text: Given clinical scenario is suggestive of Klumpke’s paralysis secondary to fall with abduction of arm causing injury to C8 and T1 nerve roots resulting in complete clawing of hand.

Erb’s Paralysis & Klumpke’s Paralysis: Feature Erb’s Paralysis Klumpke’s Paralysis Site of Injury Upper trunk of the brachial plexus (Erb’s point) Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (Option D) Causes of Injury Undue separation of head from the shoulder Birth injury/difficult childbirth During anesthesia Undue abduction of the arm Birth injury Nerve Roots Involved Mainly C5, partly C6 Mainly T1, partly C8 (Option A) Muscles Paralyzed Biceps brachii Deltoid Brachialis Brachioradialis Partly supraspinatus, infraspinatus, supinator Intrinsic muscles of the hand (T1) Ulnar flexors of the wrist and fingers (C8) Deformity and Position Arm: Hangs by the side, adducted and medially rotated Forearm: Extended and pronated (Waiter’s tip position) Also known as Policeman tip deformity Complete clawing of hand due to hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints. (Option B) Additional Features Sensory loss over lower deltoid.
Bird winging effect of scapula.
**Horner’s syndrome (Option C):** if T1 is injured. Vasomotor and trophic changes Cutaneous anesthesia along the ulnar border of the forearm and hand.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the carrying angle of the elbow is correct?

options.A: The carrying angle is formed by the angle between the humerus and the ulna when the elbow is flexed.
options.B: The carrying angle disappears during full flexion and pronation of the forearm.
options.C: The carrying angle is greater in males, usually more than 15°.
options.D: The carrying angle increases as the arm moves from full flexion to extension.

explanation.text: The carrying angle of the elbow is the angle formed between the humerus and the forearm when the arm is fully extended. This angle, typically 13°, is due to the medially and downwardly directed transverse axis of the elbow joint. The factors that contribute to this angle include: Medial flange of the trochlea being 6 mm deeper than the lateral flange. Oblique placement of the superior articular surface of the coronoid process of the ulna.
The carrying angle disappears during full flexion and pronation of the forearm, with the forearm aligning with the arm in the mid-prone position. This allows better precision in hand control.

The angle is typically 10°–15° in males and greater than 15° in females Cubitus valgus is characterized by an increased carrying angle, causing the forearm to deviate outward, while cubitus varus involves a decreased carrying angle, causing the forearm to angle inward.

questions.question: Which of the following structures can be palpated in the infraclavicular fossa ?

explanation.text: The infraclavicular fossa, also known as the deltopectoral triangle, is a triangular depression located below the junction of the lateral and middle thirds of the clavicle. It is defined by the following boundaries:

Medially: The pectoralis major muscle. Laterally: The anterior fibers of the deltoid muscle. Superiorly: The clavicle. The tip of the coracoid process of the scapula lies approximately 2–3 cm below the clavicle and is overlapped by the anterior fibers of the deltoid.

It can be felt during deep palpation just lateral to the infraclavicular fossa, which helps in locating important structures like the brachial plexus and subclavian artery in clinical assessments. This area is clinically significant for procedures such as brachial plexus block and the assessment of vascular structures like the subclavian artery.

questions.question: Identify the correctly marked attachments of the Upper end of the Humerus.

options.A: A- Supraspinatus; B- Infraspinatus; D- Pectoralis major
options.B: A- Teres minor; B- Infraspinatus; D- Subscapularis
options.C: C- Pectoralis major; D- Supraspinatus; E- Subscapularis
options.D: B- Infraspinatus; C- Pectoralis major; D- Supraspinatus

explanation.text: Upper end of Humerus: Head: The smooth, rounded head forms one-third of a sphere, covered with articular hyaline cartilage. Anatomical Neck: This constriction at the margins of the rounded head provides attachment to the capsular ligament of the shoulder joint, except at the superior region where the capsule is deficient for the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii.

Surgical Neck: A short constriction below the tubercles and epiphyseal line, where fractures are common. It is in close proximity to the axillary nerve and posterior and anterior circumflex humeral vessels. Greater Tubercle: The most lateral part of the upper end, with three flattened facets: Upper facet: Attachment for supraspinatus. Middle facet: Attachment for infraspinatus. Lower facet: Attachment for teres minor.

Mnemonic: "SIT" Lesser Tubercle: A small elevation on the front of the upper end, just above the surgical neck, providing attachment for the subscapularis muscle. Intertubercular Sulcus (Bicipital Groove): A groove between the tubercles that contains: Long head of biceps (enclosed in a synovial sheath). Ascending branch of anterior circumflex humeral artery. It provides attachment to three muscles: Pectoralis major (lateral lip).
Teres major (medial lip). Latissimus dorsi (floor). Mnemonic: "Lady between 2 Majors" (Latissimus dorsi between Pectoralis major and Teres major).

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the attachments on the coracoid process?

options.A: The short head of biceps brachii and coracobrachialis insert onto its medial border.
options.B: The conoid ligament attaches to the tip of the coracoid process.
options.C: The pectoralis minor muscle inserts onto the medial border of the upper surface.
options.D: The coracoacromial ligament attaches to the superior ridge of the coracoid process.

explanation.text: Coracoid Process Attachments: Muscle Attachments: Short head of biceps brachii and coracobrachialis arise from the tip via a common tendon. (Option A) Pectoralis minor inserts on the medial border of the upper surface.

Ligament Attachments: Coracoacromial ligament attaches to the lateral border. (Option D) Conoid ligament (part of coracoclavicular) attaches to the knuckle. (Option B) Trapezoid ligament (part of coracoclavicular) attaches to the ridge on the superior aspect. Coracohumeral ligament attaches at the root, near the glenoid cavity.

questions.question: Which of the following bones is not directly involved in the radiocarpal (wrist) joint?

explanation.text: Pisiform is a sesamoid bone located in the proximal row of the carpal bones but does not participate directly in the radiocarpal articulation. Wrist joint Synovial ellipsoidal (condyloid) joint allowing flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and circumduction. Articulating Bones The wrist joint involves the distal end of the radius and the proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum).

The ulna is not directly involved in the wrist joint but is adjacent to it, separated by an articular disc (the triangular fibrocartilage). Carpal Bones Involved Scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum are directly involved in the articulation with the radius. The pisiform is not involved in the wrist joint. Joint Capsule A fibrous joint capsule encloses the wrist joint, which is lined by a synovial membrane that produces synovial fluid for lubrication.

Ligaments Palmar radiocarpal ligament Dorsal radiocarpal ligament Ulnar collateral ligament Radial collateral ligament Movements Flexion Extension Radial deviation (abduction) Ulnar deviation (adduction) Circumduction Blood Supply The wrist joint is supplied by branches of the radial and ulnar arteries.

Nerve Supply Median nerve Ulnar nerve Radial nerve Clinical Relevance Common conditions affecting the wrist joint include wrist fractures (especially of the scaphoid and radius), carpal tunnel syndrome, and arthritis.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman falls off her bicycle and lands on her outstretched hand. She presents with pain and swelling over the lateral aspect of her wrist. On examination, there is tenderness in the anatomical snuff box. Which underlying bone is most likely fractured?

explanation.text: Tenderness in the anatomical snuff box following a fall on an outstretched hand strongly suggests a scaphoid fracture, as the scaphoid bone lies in the floor of the anatomical snuff box. Anatomical snuff box/Radial fossa: Triangular hollow visible on the lateral aspect of the wrist when the thumb is fully extended.

Boundaries: Anterolateral: Extensor pollicis brevis, Abductor pollicis longus Posteromedial: Extensor pollicis longus Roof: Dorsal cutaneous branch of radial nerve: Found in the skin and subcutaneous tissue of anatomical snuff box. Cephalic vein: Arises from dorsal venous network of hand and crosses anatomical snuff box to travel to the anterolateral aspect of forearm. Contents: Radial Artery: Crosses the floor of the anatomical snuff box.
